opening_note: October is San Diego's second summer. Some years the hottest week lands now, when the wind blows in from the desert. But the harvest has moved inland — new dates, new sweet potatoes, heavy pomegranates, the last sweet peppers — and as the water cools, the local rockfish comes in. Everything below comes from one store, and it all keeps you cooking through the week.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

field_notes.name: A new date isn't dried fruit.
field_notes.body: Most dates sit in storage for months. This fall's are softer, glossier, and taste like caramel instead of candy — squeeze the container and they give. If they're firm, dry, or have sugar crystals on the skin, they're last year's. The fresh ones are worth looking for in the bin you already shop.

field_notes.name: October is when peppers go in jars.
field_notes.body: Across the Balkans, autumn is ajvar season: red peppers are at their cheapest, and families roast them by the crate and cook them down into a relish that lasts into winter. You don't need a crate. Four peppers make a jar. It's the same impulse behind everything in this basket — buy it while it's here, and make it keep.

field_notes.name: Let the oven cut the kabocha.
field_notes.body: A kabocha is dense enough to be dangerous with a knife. Put it whole in a 400°F oven for ten minutes, or the microwave for three, and the skin softens enough to cut through safely. Don't peel it. Roasted, the skin goes tender and you eat all of it.

field_notes.name: Dry fish, hot pan, hands off.
field_notes.body: Fish sticks when it's wet or when you move it too soon. Pat it dry, salt it, heat the pan until the oil shimmers, lay the fillet down away from you, and leave it alone for three minutes. When it's ready, it lets go of the pan on its own. That's also the first step of every braise — you'll use it on bone-in chicken thighs once the evenings cool.

drink.name: Barrio Logan Jamaica
drink.intro: One drink. It's still hot, and the pomegranates just came in.
drink.method: Put the tea bags in four cups of cold water and leave them in the fridge overnight — cold-steeped, hibiscus comes out bright rather than bitter. Take out the bags. Press the seeds from one pomegranate through a strainer and stir the juice in, with sugar to taste; start with a quarter cup and stop when it's tart-sweet, not sweet. Pour over ice with a squeeze of lime and a spoonful of whole seeds. The pitcher keeps four days.

try_another_way.context: So the last glass isn't watered down.
If you want it closer to tart.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: A fresh fillet is glossy.
one_thing_to_notice.body: At the fish counter, look before you ask. Fresh fish is glossy and slightly translucent, with no gaps opening between the layers of flesh. Dull, dry, or separating means it's been sitting. Ask to smell it; it should smell like the ocean and nothing else. It takes five seconds and tells you more than any label.

meals_heading: Seven things to cook in October.
meals_dek: Specific dishes, chosen for this month's basket. Each one ends by explaining how it works — so the next time, you won't need it.

tonight.heading: Or cook by instinct
tonight.dek: When something's already in the fridge: what it wants, a few ways to cook it, and the flavors that suit it.

options.name: Rockfish
options.why: A mild fish needs something peppery and something sharp, or it tastes of nothing.

moves.text: Dry it, sear it hands-off, and flake it into warm tortillas with something cold and sharp.
Sear it and finish it in brown butter and lemon, over roasted squash.
Leftovers: flake it cold onto oiled toast with arugula and lemon.

options.name: Chicken sausage
options.why: It brings its own fat — let that fat cook the vegetables.

moves.text: Roast it on one hot pan with squash and peppers, then add something smoky.
Leftovers: slice it into a skillet with cubed sweet potato until it all crisps, and crack an egg on top.

options.name: Pork tenderloin
options.why: Lean meat gets its richness from the finish, not the pan.

moves.text: Roast it hot, pull it while it's pink, and cover it in something sweet, salty, and oily.
Leftovers: slice it thin over rice with ajvar and arugula.

options.name: Ground lamb
options.why: Rich, slightly gamey meat wants sweet and sour against it.

moves.text: Brown it hard until it crusts, and spoon it over cold salted yogurt with fruit.
Pile it into a split baked sweet potato with feta and dates.

options.name: Eggs and beans
options.why: The cheapest dinners want the most flavor — the jar's smoke and something cool.

moves.text: Crisp sourdough in olive oil, spread the jar thick, and top it with runny eggs.
Bake sweet potatoes until the sugar runs and fill them with warm beans.
Cube any leftover squash or potato, crisp it in a skillet, and crack eggs into the pan.

flavors.name: Smoky
flavors.how: A spoonful of the jar and its oil, lemon squeezed over everything.

flavors.name: Cool and sharp
flavors.how: Yogurt on the plate first, the hot food on top, seeds over it all.

flavors.name: Bright and hot
flavors.how: Warm olive oil with a grated garlic clove and chile flakes for one minute. Pour it over; squeeze lime hard.

flavors.name: Sweet and salty
flavors.how: Torn dates and crumbled feta, a pinch of chile so it isn't dessert.
